This arrangement allows MIMO pairs to share the same resource while utilizing their individual transfer functions. Our work focuses on the optimal power allocation for maximizing MIMO two-way sum-rate, given the constraints of individual MIMO pair capacities. Our investigation into highly adaptive measurements led us to a new set of measurements known as generalized orthogonal measurements (GOMs). We evaluate the impact of background topologies, particularly those induced by the weak charge, on precision measurements of the weak mixing angle in both charged current and neutral current experiments. We investigate three significant non-Oscillation-Associated Topologies (OAST) contribution structures: those stemming from the weak charge, the CKM matrix, and parton distribution functions respectively. We assess the OAST effects on the weak mixing angle determination in DUNE and DUSF experiments at various distances from the neutrino source. The analysis reveals that the dominant error source in the mixing angle measurement arises from the weak charge contribution, accounting for up to 40% of the total systematic uncertainty at 1300 km. We suggest that by accurately modelling the weak charge contribution, the systematic uncertainty in the mixing angle measurement can be reduced. This is particularly relevant, as the weak charge contribution is expected to be more prominent in DUNE's iron target data rather than in liquid argon data. We outline possible experimental strategies to validate the weak charge contribution and thereby verify the parton distribution functions. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for extracting parton distribution functions from the data, leveraging the weak charge contribution and neutrino oscillations in conjunction with CDF data on the gluon distribution function. This approach is expected to provide significant improvements in the parton distribution function precision, particularly for the strange and sea quark distributions, with down-flepton distribution function precision improvements of two orders of magnitude. This achievement is anticipated to have a substantial impact in various fields, particularly high-energy physics, hadron physics and precision physics, with potential breakthroughs in the study of the Drell-Yan process, electromagnetic form factors and parton distribution functions. But what if you could train a model to grasp objects in any shape without being simplified? We've made significant progress in this area by developing a GAN-based approach that allows the learning of policies directly from raw perception without pre-existing models or simplifications. Our method, which is based on enhanced Generative Adversarial Networks, has enabled the creation of policies that can learn from raw perception and has been successfully applied to two challenging robotic tasks: grasping objects of varying shapes and sizes, and assembly grasping, where the training data includes images from real-world agents. By using GANs to learn from raw perception, we've been able to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms that use pre-existing object models without simplifications. Additionally, our approach allows the generation of diverse policies by sampling from a learned distribution, which can be difficult with traditional optimization-based methods. However, as shown in Figure 2, the diversity of the policies generated can be limited by the challenge's complexity, leading to a trade-off between policy diversity and the network's capacity. Finally, our approach has been shown to outperform previous GAN-based methods, where the added constraint of learning a meaningful prior has a positive effect on the performance of the policy learning algorithm. But what's more surprising is that this effect occurs even when the prior is not directly related to the policy or the data, where the key factor appears to be the regularizing effect on the network's latent space rather than the prior itself. Which brings us to a set of experiments where we've been able to replicate the same regularizing effect using a normalizing flow network that maps a uniform distribution to a meaningful prior, where the meaningfulness of the prior is subjective. Overall, our research has been successful in breaking free from the limitations of blockworld and has significant implications for a range of areas including reinforcement learning, where the model's structure is separate from the state and action spaces, and generative modeling, where the network's capacity can be difficult to utilize effectively. We view the system as a first-order ODE in a 5-dimensional space with a non-smooth nonlinear vector field and a polyhedral bundle. We create a multigrid solver that converges in a unified manner to all equilibrium points of the system. We then apply the method to a specific Voronoi mesh in two dimensions and test the solver with various initial conditions, demonstrating its ability to accurately achieve a precise convergence of ten decimal places for most points, albeit with a slightly reduced precision at a singular equilibrium point. We outline the general approach for extending the multigrid method in three spatial dimensions and discuss the potential challenges and advantages of the solver in three dimensions. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence of the multigrid method in any number of dimensions, taking into account the non-smoothness of the vector field and the singularities of the equilibrium set. The theoretical results are based on a model of the circuit in three dimensions and assume that the boundaries of the circuit are defined by a smooth equation. We believe that the proposed multigrid method is the first of its kind for a non-smooth nonlinear system of PDEs/ODEs, although it can also be applied to a smooth nonlinear system of ODEs. We highlight the main difficulty in applying the multigrid method in three dimensions, namely the non-smoothness of the vector field due to the jump discontinuity across Voronoi boundaries, and outline potential solutions to mitigate this issue. We finally discuss the computational advantages of the proposed multiguid method in terms of energy reduction and convergence to equilibrium, and suggest that the method may also have implications for data analysis, as the Port-Hamiltonian system can be used to model complex relationships between variables in a dataset. We take a dataset on US income from the US Census Bureau as an example and model the relationship between the variables using a 2D Port-Hamiltonian system, applying the multigrid method to solve the system. This work presents a comprehensive empirical assessment of semi-supervised transfer learning, evaluating its performance on a range of benchmark datasets and showcasing its potential to improve the efficiency and robustness of online training, particularly when online samples are limited. HASHTAG's novel architecture leverages the dual nature of the language model, utilizing its text generation capabilities while adopting a hierarchical sampling method to process input sequences. By doing so, HASHTAG successfully captures comprehensive failure patterns across various context spans. Thorough evaluations have been conducted to assess the performance of HASHTAG and compare it to existing methods. Notably, when tested on the LMF dataset, HASHTAG demonstrates superior predictive capabilities, achieving a 0.2034 micro-F1 score, while fine-tuning the models results in an even higher 0.2081 micro-F1 score, indicating a notable improvement of 2.6% over the previous state-of-the-art. Extensive analysis and ablation studies have been carried out to examine the behavior and adaptability of the model. Based on these findings, the theoretical advantages and empirical results suggest that language models can effectively identify complex failure patterns across diverse context spans. Moreover, these capabilities not only enhance the quality of generated text but also contribute to the robustness of the model. As a result, the data seen by the model during pre-training can actually improve its failure detection performance. Interestingly, the impact of text length on failure prediction reveals an inverse relationship, where longer texts exhibit lower failure rates, which aligns with expectations. Lastly, the class activation maps generated by HASHTAG provide valuable insights into its internal workings and demonstrate a strong correlation with the models it was trained on, confirming the reliability of the model. Video demonstrations and additional resources are available online. The project's code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepCaret/HASHTAG. As an important contribution to the field, we have successfully developed an end-to-end failure prediction model trained on language models, which significantly addresses a long-standing challenge. As the first model of its kind, HASHTAG opens up new avenues for future research in this area. One potential direction for further investigation involves leveraging HASHTAG's failure predictions to adapt the model's training configuration and improve its overall performance. Ultimately, the development of HASHTAG represents an important milestone toward achieving more robust and intelligent AI systems. This study focuses on a particular type of normalization, known as the tanh normalization, which involves applying the hyperbolic tangent function to a given value, constraining it between -1 and 1. We have investigated the effects of preprocessing data using tanh normalization on the performance of deep neural networks representing large-size graphs. Our research involves comparing different approaches for converting graph attributes and modeling user and item representations, and we found that applying tanh normalization improves performance on the large real-world Amazon datasets. Our study demonstrates that even simple data normalization techniques can be crucial for successful large-scale graph representation learning. This code is part of a larger project on graph representation learning, which can be found at this link: https://github.com/jparchetto/graph-representation-learning. This study was conducted as part of a larger research project on graph representation learning, and the related paper has been submitted to the 15th Workshop on Advances in Broad-Band Networks, ABBN 2022. Following the workshop, this paper will be published in the ABBN 2022 proceedings. We have also included an abstract based on the related paper below. 

Abstract: 
Deep neural networks have been applied to graph modeling tasks but face significant resource constraints due to large graph sizes. This study investigates the effect of data normalization on deep neural network performance representing large-size graphs. Our experiments involve modeling Amazon product networks, and the results demonstrate that applying tanh normalization improves the accuracy of our models. This study contributes to the body of research on graph representation learning, and the associated code will be made open-source to facilitate further exploration. 

Keywords: graph representation learning, deep neural networks, data normalization.

In contrast, this study examines daily loads and examines model choices as well as the potential for enhancing load uncertainty models. The analysis is grounded in a large-scale probabilistic load forecasting dataset for Austria, covering a five-year period and involving over 4,000 municipalities. In addition, various methods for extracting features from the data are examined, with the inclusion of meteorological time-series yielding the lowest log-sharp-Shen consistency scores. The study's best model achieves an average log-sharp-Shen consistency score of 1.46. The findings also suggest that daily load forecasts could be enhanced by incorporating spatial information about neighboring municipalities, with the model performing better for municipalities surrounded by a high number of similar neighboring towns. The study provides a flexible framework for generating uncertainty visualizations and identifies several key insights about the relationship between load and spatial proximity. To achieve this, we compiled a dataset consisting of 50 concepts with multiple occurrences and mapped them to their corresponding semantic frameworks. In response, we developed a streamlined, end-to-end workflow centered on the concept of "common knowledge" to facilitate collaboration and optimal data use. Researchers have extensively explored methods like fixed rank core tensor decomposition for reducing rank in tensors. However, these approaches often rely on an a priori rank estimate, which can be challenging to determine. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed core tensor projections that adapt to the intrinsic rank of a core tensor. This study introduces a new type of core tensor projection called the hyperbolic embedding-based core tensor projection (HEP), derived from hyperbolic embeddings. Unlike existing adaptive core tensor projections, HEP is uniquely positioned as both a minimization of a core tensor's norm and a minimization of a corresponding multilinear function's norm, where this minimization adapts to the intrinsic rank of the core tensor. To evaluate HEP, researchers developed a hyperbolic embedding-based HEP algorithm (GEH) and tested it on synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing its performance to alternative methods. These sources appear as persistent, extended, kiloparsec-scale structures known as extended narrow emission-line regions (ENERMs) or striations in X-ray and UV spectra. Previous studies of ENERMs in powerful radio sources revealed X-ray and UV continuum emissions that were similar in shape and spectrum, leading researchers to conclude they were produced by the same mechanism. However, by closely examining the X-ray and UV spectra of ENERMs, this study shows that the narrow X-ray band is likely caused by thermal comptonization of the seed photons from the flat UV continuum, whereas the broad X-ray band is produced by relativistic electrons interacting with the seed photons through synchrotron radiation. The X-ray continuum of ENERMs is observable because it is much stronger than in quiescent narrow emission-line regions (NENRs). The broad power-law X-ray emissions of NENRs are thought to be the jets' X-ray counterparts, but the UV continuum of NENRs is too bright for the seed photons of the narrow X-ray band to dominate the X-ray energy balance. Therefore, the narrow X-ray band produced by NERMs cannot be the jet X-ray counterpart. The discovery of these X-ray producing mechanisms in ENERMs implies that the jets' roles in powering the UV and X-ray emissions of powerful radio sources are less significant than previously thought. As a result, the theory that jets are responsible for both the UV and X-ray emissions of these radio sources should be revised. The findings of these studies also provide insights into the physical conditions in the ENERMs, which are consistent with being quiescent regions of powerful extragalactic radio sources. The study also highlights the importance of understanding the UV producing mechanisms in ENERMs in determining the properties of their X-ray producing mechanisms. By combining X-ray and UV spectral information, the properties of the X-ray producing mechanisms can be constrained, which in turn allows researchers to determine the maximum jet power and synchrotron radiation energy production efficiency. This paper proposes an innovative approach to language adaptation, splitting it into two sub-problems: covering language families common in emerging markets and developing a compact model capable of handling phonetic-based translation. To tackle the first issue, we introduce a framework for creating multi-domain specific mask token generation, building on existing CTRG and fine-tuning the model with labeled data. Various metrics have been developed to measure functional complexity, but most existing methods are either data-metric, meaning they rely on task-specific datasets, or only account for one aspect of complexity. This paper introduces RandoNet, a novel neural network-enabling method that measures the input space diversity of a function computed by a neural network. By utilizing this method, we analyzed the complexity evolution during training for multiple CNNs configured in different ways on ImageNet, revealing significant complexity disparities even within the same network configured differently. Our findings also indicate that maximizing functional diversity is key to achieving generalization. Additionally, we employed RandoNet to evaluate the fairness of neural network assignments and discovered that fair assignments can sometimes result in lower error rates, but at the cost of lower diversity. This highlights the need to balance error and diversity considerations. As an application, we used RandoNet to develop an adaptive neural network optimization technique that leverages diversity to guide the optimization process, resulting in improved generalization. By assessing RandoNet on various benchmark datasets, we demonstrated that the optimally diverse solution often or almost always achieves lower error rates, confirming the importance of functional diversity. This study is available at https://github.com/chenzhaoyu1997/RandoNet. Its code can be used to measure the diversity of functions computed by neural networks, both synthetic and real-world, trained with various optimizers and algorithms, and across multiple input dimensions. Our method can also be used to measure the complexity of other machine learning models and algorithms. Our goal is to develop a set of tools that enable researchers to study and utilize functional diversity in machine learning systems. Our long-term vision is to develop a framework for measuring and analyzing the overall functional complexity of machine learning systems, which in turn may reveal new dimensions for risk assessment. This study develops a joint model for identifying the parties involved in news articles and the perspectives expressed towards them. Using a trained model, we annotated 2,457 Wall Street Journal articles related to five significant U.S. political scandals between 1985-2015. Notably, our findings show that the public reaction to these scandals was complex and multifaceted, with different media outlets expressing varying perspectives. While The New York Times generally condemned the Nixon administration over Watergate, for instance, it had mixed opinions, with some articles blaming the government and others focusing on other aspects. In contrast, the Washington Post primarily emphasized government culpability in its coverage of Watergate. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for the influence of secondary parties, such as other government officials, experts, and organizations, in news articles. By doing so, we gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex evolution of public perception during these scandals. Our research methodology and data analysis code are available for others to access. However, our results also underscore the challenges associated with accurately annotating news articles manually, particularly when dealing with complex topics like public corruption. Finally, we explore the potential of our approach as a benchmark for future automated annotation systems. Our data is now publicly available through the Penn Data Archive. Our proposed framework consists of three essential components: 1) A memory system called Conversational Context Memory (CCMem) that stores, retains, and updates contextual representations for each conversation. 2) A task classifier that uses the learned CLIP features to detect task transitions and triggers contextual memory updates. 3) A shared, fine-tuned dialogue manager (SharedDA) applicable to all tasks, which utilizes both historical responses and preserved contextual representations. Researchers have developed various attacks against audio recognition systems, but most of these focus on manipulating the device's input by playing pre-designed malicious sounds. Our research takes a different approach, exploring the potential consequences of the audio processing module when it is not under external attack. Specifically, we discovered that intelligent speakers and smartphones can inadvertently reveal sensitive user information using only legitimate sounds, such as a user's voice, music stored locally, or streaming content. We developed SoundEx, an technique that utilizes machine learning to show that these intelligent devices can be used to gather sensitive user information, such as their location, identity, or activity. SoundEx operates by extracting acoustic features from speech and non-speech sounds, and then using a neural network to connect these features to specific categories. Our research shows that these intelligent devices can be used to identify users, recognize their voice, and stream content, and that existing noise-reducing methods do not effectively protect against this type of attack. Our findings highlight the need for new protection mechanisms to prevent the misuse of audio intelligence. SoundEx source code is available upon request. Although GANs have achieved remarkable success in the creation of realistic data representations, they often struggle with stability during training due to their non-solvable, non-convex nature. To address this issue, training methods like virtual gradient descent and its variants propose solving non-convex problems using stabilizing techniques based on adversarial training. In contrast, this study introduces a new learning framework, which leverages adversarial training to derive a consistent, stable representation of data through adversarial regularizers. This approach builds on the idea that data distribution can be approximated using a simple distribution such as Gaussian, and we can remove noise by dismissing distribution outliers. This goal is achieved by applying quantile loss to eliminate noise and improve data representation, which leads to the proposed framework named PC-GAN. nanophotonics is crucial for developing quantum light sources and for enhancing non-classical light-matter interactions in solid-state media. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate a new approach to creating individual quantum emitters by tailoring the design of a deep nanoscale hole array. By optimizing the hole design, we enhance the interactions between the dipole inducements of the holes during laser crystallization, resulting in a highly synchronized quantum state among these inducements. This, in turn, enables the controlled extraction of a strong, directional photonic signal from the hole array. Notably, the measured second-order correlation function confirmed the quantum nature of this photonic signal. Computational models of the arrays support the experimental findings and offer insights into optimizing the platform for generating photonic signals of varying properties. The platform offers a promising solution for producing quantum light sources and for exploring non-traditional light behaviors in engineered photonic systems. The technology has potential uses in fields like quantum communication, biological sensing, and data storage. The platform may also be applied to the creation of miniaturized photonic circuits for manipulating light at the nanoscale. The study demonstrates the feasibility of producing such circuits using current fabrication techniques. The arrays exhibit an unusual combination of properties: deep holes typically serve as photonic sensors, but in this case, they also emit photons. This unusual behavior stems from the precise arrangement of the holes and the optimization of the light interactions among them, effectively 'coupling' the holes together. The combination of Monte Carlo simulation and implicit neural networks (INNs) offers a flexible framework for modeling various types of PDEs. However, previous research encountered difficulties in training INNs when working with real-world data, primarily due to the limited availability of observed state variables. In this paper, we address these challenges by presenting an end-to-end training approach for the solution of forward and inverse problems involving partial differential equations. The proposed strategy involves initial input processing steps, followed by the integration of neural ordinary differential equations and finite difference methods to approximate the solution of forward and inverse Advection-Diffusion equations. The results show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, while also enhancing the overall efficiency of the solution process. A recent study by Hallewellyn et al. (2021) explored how effectively these replacement pairs convey the notion of similarity, and how naturally they are perceived by individuals familiar with the relevant languages. To assess this, they developed an innovative metric that measures the similarity of concepts based on their semantic meanings, and created a corpus of image descriptions from Wikipedia to test the effectiveness of these replacement pairs in representing similar but distinct concepts. Notably, the results showed that "day" and "night" scored slightly higher on average than other language-neutral or English-based pairs such as "space and heaven," "big and small," "light and heavy," and "love and heart." Interestingly, the most successful pair scored a 0.187 in our metric, indicating a clear distinction between the concepts replaced. The authors also analyzed the types of situations in which "like night and day" is commonly used and how its replacement pair "como la noche y el día" fares comparably in Spanish. To facilitate future research, they provide access to the code, data, and image description corpus used in their study. As idiomatic expressions play a vital role in language, the authors hope that their work will contribute to a greater understanding of how these complex phrases can be effectively employed in both language generation and understanding tasks. Firstly, we identify a correlation between continuum temperature and ionization stage, with higher stages exhibiting higher temperatures. Secondly, we observe a positive correlation between temperature and ionization parameter (fi) in highly ionized objects but a negative correlation in less ionized objects. Our characterization of quasar hot flows aligns with simulations of AGN, with both simulations and observations displaying similar temperature and ionization parameter dynamics. These findings collectively enhance our understanding of quasar hot flows. It outlines a strategy for developing a "GAGA for $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois theory', which involves  linking $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois groups to harmonic analysis on quasi-Poincaré duality groups, specifically through their representation theories.  By considering the former as an extension of the latter, we aim to establish a "GAGA correspondence' that equates quasi-Poincaré duality groups with $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois groups.  This correspondence is expected to hold constant dimension and cover similarities.  As an initial step, a 'coarse' version of GAGA is provided, which focuses on the classification of $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois groups through their maximal regular subgroups.  This is grounded in an analysis of regular subgroups of Poincaré duality groups, which is itself a continuation of earlier work.  Building on the 2008 comparison theorem of Ichino-Murty-Sudler, a local duality result is established, which is used to show the existence and uniqueness of regular subgroups of Poincaré duality groups.  The properties of these regular subgroups are then studied, and a continuation of the work of Rickert reveals that their maximal subgroups possess similar properties.  By applying this 'coarse' version of GAGA, we aim to establish a 'fine' version, which is expected to yield a comprehensive classification of $\mathbb{Q}$-Galois groups through their maximal regular subgroups.  This is expected to be complemented by a classification of quasi-Poincaré duality groups through their minimal p-local subgroups.  As an alternative, a local approach may be taken, which is expected to be more flexible but also less developed.  The text is divided into four main sections, which cover the background, the coarseness, the fineness, and the unicity of GAGA.  A comprehensive outline of GAGA is provided in the appendix, which is expected to serve as a foundation for future developments.  The text includes numerous examples and open questions. Assuming a "strict strong convex ratio" in their objective function, we show that a particular saddlepoint approximation yields an optimal solution that also satisfies strict feasibility, thereby obtaining two-sided error bounds for its duality gap. Furthermore, we establish that this saddlepoint approximation is dual to a standard piecewise linear relaxation of the original optimization problem. Moreover, by discretizing the approximation along its duality gap, ranging from infinity to zero, we obtain an infinite series of piecewise linear relaxations whose values converge to the original optimization problem's value. In addition, we demonstrate that each iteration yields an upper bound to the previous one, thereby resulting in a sequence of decreasing upper bounds to the original optimization problem's value. Our theoretical findings are supported through various numerical experiments. In these, we considered three different saddlepoint approximations associated with linear optimization, namely, the Lagrangization, Tikhonov regularization of Lagrangian relaxation, as well as the Linearization method. Our numerical studies show that these methods provide good quality upper bounds to the actual optimization problem's value, often better than other available approaches. In particular, we observed that the Linearization method tends to perform more efficiently than Lagrangization through a smaller number of iterations. Moreover, we found that Tikhonov regularization of Lagrangian relaxation yields an improved Tikhonov regularization of the standard piecewise linear relaxation, resulting in reduced computation times compared to direct evaluation on the piecewise linear relaxation, with a particular advantage in problems featuring at most two pieces. known as counterfactual learning (Kaplan et al., 2017), aims to forecast the consequences of various actions made over a system's current state. Present counterfactual models often struggle with complex scenarios, such as large action pools and intricate environmental relationships. Our research introduces a novel hierarchical framework, called Counterfactual Learning by World Exploration (CLoBE), addressing these limitations. CLoBE employs a top-level module for planning and exploring the most relevant actions, while using a bottom-level module for simulating the environmental responses to these chosen actions. Specifically, CLoBE leverages the options framework (Sutton et al., 1999) to train an exploration module that selects actions leading to significant changes and reduced redundancy. Our experimental evaluation confirms that CLoBE effectively discovers low-regret policies in challenging scenarios involving large action spaces. Moreover, CLoBE successfully identifies the most influential actions and explores the environmental dynamics, providing easily accessible understanding of the learned policies. We demonstrate the practical value of CLoBE in scenarios where human counterfactual learning is difficult due to limited data availability, such as visual question-answering and visual reasoning. However, due to limitations imposed by hardware and data transfer limitations, it is often necessary to simulate real-world examples in order to train these networks. Ideally, a simulation model should accurately replicate the target environment in every detail, but in practice, this is rarely the case. Typically, simulation models contain both accurate representations of the target environment and inaccuracies introduced by limitations, which can be categorized as either random or systematic errors. While random errors dissipate as more data is generated, systematic errors create biases that are consistent across the simulated data. For instance, a camera simulation might always simulate the camera's position on the right side due to limitations, or a racing car simulation might always show the road on the right side due to a bug, or accurately replicate the real world's driving conditions. We refer to any simulation model that introduces systematic errors as flawed. In this research, we demonstrate that training Deep Neural Networks using data generated by flawed simulation models can result in a significant loss in performance of at least 30% even for simple models and even when a limited amount of real-world data is available even if the source of the error can be identified. We present a robust, efficient method for detecting these types of errors called SED, which uses neural networks to isolate and eliminate the impact of these errors. We then show that our method allows the creation of Deep Neural Networks that are not only resilient to these types of errors but also perform optimally on both the flawed simulation data as well as real-world data. Notably, our method requires minimal information and can be applied to various types of errors. We believe this method to be universally applicable to other problems involving estimation and optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using various real-world examples including a well-known issue with facial recognition where the model would incorrectly identify a person's gender based on a photo taken from the side, another example where the model would incorrectly identify an object's type based on a photo taken from the side despite having access to real-world data, and an example where the model would incorrectly identify an object's type based on a photo taken from the side due to a bug in the real-world data. Validation of our method using actual data from the KITTI dataset shows that our method allows the creation of Deep Neural Networks that perform optimally on the real-world data. We provide a concise history of RNNs and discovered that fundamental aspects of RNNs were previously overlooked, contributing to training difficulties. We identified that RNNs are essentially Convex Recurrent Networks (CRNs) with locally convex objectives in standard cases. Our empirical findings also demonstrate that standard gradient descent can train CRNs and non-convex RNNs effectively, but local convergence may not always occur. To address this, we propose a gradient clipping method, which can lead to local convergence in non-convex RNNs. The model's intricate state transitions, involving multiple Markov systems that switch dynamically, make finding its maximum likelihood parameterization nearly impossible with traditional gradient-based methods. To overcome this challenge, we propose a line search constrained L-BFGS algorithm for MS-MS models. The L-BFGS method is known for its fast convergence, even in non-convex regions, and we adapt it for MS-MS maximum likelihood estimation by constraining each iteration with a gradient-based loss function. The numerical results demonstrate that our approach converges rapidly to a local optimum, achieving a convergence rate of at least O(1/k) with a statistical bias of O(1/k^(1/2)), outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, the algorithm takes advantage of MS-MS model properties to precisely compute the Hessian matrix of the objective function, providing an accurate gradient estimate and improved convergence. The algorithm's efficiency is further enhanced by only computing necessary state transition probabilities, reducing computational complexity and making it scalable for real-world applications. To verify its effectiveness, we apply the algorithm to a financial time series dataset and compare its results with alternative methods based on genetic algorithms or simulated annealing, demonstrating its superior performance. The algorithm's ability to identify dynamic regime changes enables a more thorough understanding of the financial time series' behavior, and the temporal analysis of the model's log-likelihood surface reveals that only this algorithm successfully captures the model's complex features. Common methods like HDR offloading and screen-space ambient occlusion render maps at a lower resolution than the final image, but this can cause visible artifacts, pixelation, and slow performance. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an innovative HDR compression technique that not only maintains the original lighting details but also coalesces mesh triangles to contribute to a significant reduction in rendering latency. Our method, an adjustable and efficient low-variability HDR filter, can be applied either pre- or post-rendering to produce a range of smooth and detailed outputs, and is accompanied by a fast post-process re-rendering algorithm to ensure seamless integration with existing rendering pipelines, including volumetric effects and atmospheric scattering. Our experimental results showcase a substantial visual improvement over current approaches, and demonstrate a significant performance gain, particularly for complex scenes with high-resolution textures and high-frequency volumetric effects. Our technology has been successfully deployed on the Oculus Quest VR headset. Our code is available on GitHub under the MIT open-source license. Our video showcases several key findings, highlighting the trade-offs between performance and high-frequency details under different lighting conditions, demonstrating the significant visual improvements achievable through mesh coalescence, and showing how our low-variability HDR filter enables a wide range of sophisticated global illumination effects that would otherwise be impossible to produce in real-time. Our data sets, consisting of various 3D scenes, lighting conditions, and HDR maps, have been made available on the Standard Tobacco data repository, enabling the reproducibility of our experiments and allowing other researchers to explore different combinations of mesh coalescence, filtering, and re-rendering approaches to produce a range of visually appealing outcomes. Our work has significant implications for the development of real-time global illumination techniques, and we believe that providing researchers with a controllable and adjustable tool for producing a wide variety of visually appealing effects will foster innovation and drive the advancement of this field.
